title: Pacific Crest Trail Association
wikitext:
{{short description|Non-profit organization in the US}}{{Use mdy dates|date=February 2026}} {{Infobox organization | name = Pacific Crest Trail Association | formation = 1992 (as Pacific Crest Trail Association)
1971 (as Pacific Crest Trail Club) | logo = | abbreviation = PCTA | type = [[Nonprofit organization]] | purpose = Conservation and management of the [[Pacific Crest Trail]] | headquarters = [[Sacramento, California]], [[United States]] | region_served = [[California]]; [[Oregon]]; [[Washington (state)|Washington]] | methods = Trail maintenance; volunteer coordination; education; advocacy; land acquisition | key_people = Liz Bergeron (former Executive Director) | parent_organization = | affiliations = [[United States Forest Service]]; [[National Park Service]]; [[Bureau of Land Management]]; [[California Department of Parks and Recreation]] | website = | executive_director = }} '''The Pacific Crest Trail Association''' (PCTA) is a nonprofit organization dedicated to the conservation and management of the [[Pacific Crest Trail|Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail]] (usually abbreviated as the PCT), a 2,650-mile hiking and equestrian trail in the western United States that runs through California, Oregon, and Washington. The southern terminus is in [[Campo, California]] at the Mexican border approximately 50 miles east of San Diego. The northern terminus is at the US–Canadian border at [[E. C. Manning Provincial Park|E.C. Manning Provincial Park]], which lies just north of the border between Washington and [[British Columbia]]. == History == The PCT was established as a national scenic trail by the [[National Trails System|National Trails Systems Act]] of 1968. In 1971, the Pacific Crest Trail Club was founded, and in 1977 the Pacific Crest Trail Conference was incorporated. The two groups merged in 1987, and in 1992, the name was changed to the Pacific Crest Trail Association. The Association hired its first paid staff in 1993.{{Cite web|title=Brief History of the Pacific Crest Trail|url=https://blog.theclymb.com/out-there/brief-history-pacific-crest-trail/|website=The Clymb|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2022-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/https://blog.theclymb.com/out-there/brief-history-pacific-crest-trail/|url-status=live}} The PCTA works under a [[Memorandum of understanding|Memorandum of Understanding]]{{Cite web|title=Memorandum of Understanding|url=https://www.pcta.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/11/PCTA_MOU_executed.20150512.pdf|website=US Government Documents via PCTA|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2020-11-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112025212/https://www.pcta.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/11/PCTA_MOU_executed.20150512.pdf|url-status=live}} with the U.S.D.A Forest Service (the lead agency responsible for governmental oversight of the trail), and other federal agencies.{{Cite web|title=Pacific Crest Trail|url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/pct|website=U.S.D.A. Forest Service|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2022-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043117/https://www.fs.usda.gov/pct|url-status=live}}{{Cite web|title=PCTA Partnerships|url=https://www.pcta.org/our-work/partnerships/agency-partners/|website=PCTA|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2022-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/https://www.pcta.org/our-work/partnerships/agency-partners/|url-status=live}} The PCTA is headquartered in Sacramento, California. == Mission and partnerships == The PCTA's mission is to protect, preserve and promote the Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail as a world-class experience for hikers and equestrians, and for all the values provided by wild and scenic lands.{{Cite web|title=The Pacific Crest Trail|url=http://www.sierraculture.com/visitors/pacific-crest-trail/|website=Sierra Culture|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2022-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/http://www.sierraculture.com/visitors/pacific-crest-trail/|url-status=live}} The [[United States Forest Service|USDA Forest Service]], the governmental agency charged with overseeing federal oversight of the trail, elaborates that the PCTA fulfills this mission by 1) promoting the use and protection of the Pacific Crest Trail to reflect its world-class significance for the enjoyment, education and adventure of hikers and equestrians 2) publishing information on the PCT including books, guidebooks, maps, condition reports, videos, and permits 3) sponsoring a wide variety of public service volunteer projects and programs in cooperation with agency partners such as the USDA-Forest Service, the [[National Park Service]], the [[Bureau of Land Management]], [[California State Parks]], and others.{{Cite web|title=The Pacific Crest Trail Association|url=http://www.fs.usda.gov/r05/angeles|website=U.S.D.A. Forest Service, Angeles National Forest|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2022-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043116/https://www.fs.usda.gov/detail/angeles/?cid=STELPRDB5195835|url-status=live}} In 2021, along with the USDA Forest Service and the National Park Service, the PCTA collaborated on a Foundation Document to identify the significance of and fundamental resources for the entire 2,650 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT). The project considers the perspectives of stakeholders and organizations including the U.S.D.A. Forest Service, the National Park Service, the Bureau of Land Management, California State Parks, the PTCA, Backcountry Horseman of America, 60 Indian tribes whose current and ancestral lands are along the trail, hiking clubs, volunteers, thru-hikers, trail towns, and others.{{Cite web|title=Foundation Document|url=https://www.nps.gov/articles/pct_foundation_document.htm|website=National Park Service|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2022-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043116/https://www.nps.gov/articles/pct_foundation_document.htm|url-status=live}} == Education and trail support activities == The PCTA serves as a clearinghouse for information about trail conditions, threats to the trails, and issues that affect hikers and equestrians. In 2019, the [[The Trust for Public Land|Trust for Public Land]] announced that in partnership with the PCTA, it had protected 17 miles of trail in northern California, and identified [[climate change]] and fires, timber cutting, increased usage, threats to wildlife from human interaction, and maintaining funding from the federally administered [[Land and Water Conservation Fund]] as key management priorities.{{Cite web|title=Five Threats to the Pacific Crest Trail and How We Are Fighting Back|url=https://www.tpl.org/blog/five-threats-pacific-crest-trail-and-how-we’re-fighting-back|website=Trust for Public Lands|access-date=2022-02-19|archive-date=2022-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129081113/https://www.tpl.org/blog/five-threats-pacific-crest-trail-and-how-we%E2%80%99re-fighting-back|url-status=live}} Through media campaigns and its own outreach, the PCTA educates hikers about issues that affect the trail. These issues can include temporary closures, or can be more global. For example, the PCT makes hikers aware of how climate change is affecting large-scale western forest fires, which can destroy hundreds of miles of trail and create life-threatening conditions that force hikers to abandon their itineraries.{{Cite web|last=Harrell|first=Ashley|date=Aug 4, 2021|title=Hiking the Pacific Crest Trail is 'almost impossible' due to climate change|url=https://www.sfgate.com/california-parks/article/Pacific-Crest-Trail-thru-hike-climate-change-fires-16364571.php|website=SF Gate|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043117/https://www.sfgate.com/california-parks/article/Pacific-Crest-Trail-thru-hike-climate-change-fires-16364571.php|url-status=live}} Additionally, the PCTA website contains comprehensive information about trail closures, conditions, relocations, events, books, maps, and upcoming trail events that educate hikers in safe backcountry travel and [[Leave No Trace]] principles. In 2017, in cooperation with some of its donors, it operated a program it called P3 (Preserve, Protect, and Promote—taken from its mission statement), which highlighted ten Pacific Crest Trail thru-hikers who would help promote and advocate for the PCT via blogs and social media during their thru-hikes.{{Cite web|last=Bauer|first=Brian|date=Apr 12, 2017|title=P3 Hiker program promotes awareness of responsible use of the Pacific Crest Trail|url=https://www.outsidebusinessjournal.com/press-releases/p3-hiker-program-promotes-awareness-of-responsible-use-of-the-pacific-crest-trail-2/|website=Outside Business Journal|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/https://www.outsidebusinessjournal.com/press-releases/p3-hiker-program-promotes-awareness-of-responsible-use-of-the-pacific-crest-trail-2/|url-status=live}} == Trail maintenance and continuity == The Pacific Crest Trail Association takes a lead role in maintaining the trail and keeping it open and passable as a continuous foot and bridle path from Mexico to Canada. Maintaining the trail requires clearing undergrowth and fallen trees, repairing damage from storms and flooding, building new trail that needs to be relocated because of damage, treadway improvement, or land ownership issues; and maintaining trail signage. Speaking as the executive director of the PCTA in 2016, Liz Bergeron, told [[ESPN]] that PCTA volunteers logged 96,500 hours in the previous year, the majority of which were spent on trail maintenance. She estimated that PCTA volunteers probably covered about 50 percent of what is needed every year, or about 1300 miles of the trail's nearly 2700 mile length.{{Cite web|last=Williams|first=Doug|title=Liz Bergeron's Cool Sports Job: Pacific Crest Trail Association Executive Director|url=https://www.espn.com/espnw/voices/story/_/id/17672360/liz-bergeron-cool-sports-job-pacific-crest-trail-association-executive-director|website=ESPN|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2022-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043117/https://www.espn.com/espnw/voices/story/_/id/17672360/liz-bergeron-cool-sports-job-pacific-crest-trail-association-executive-director|url-status=live}} The PCTA additionally runs a trail skills course that educates volunteers about trail maintenance, tools, and safety.{{Cite web|title=Trail Skills College Course|url=https://www.pcta.org/volunteer/trail-skills-college/trail-skills-college-course-curriculum/|website=PCTA|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2022-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043119/https://www.pcta.org/volunteer/trail-skills-college/trail-skills-college-course-curriculum/|url-status=live}} The PCTA has also had a role in protecting the integrity of the trail as a continuous footpath, for example, negotiating easements and trail routings with private landowners. While a Golden Spike ceremony in 1993 celebrated the completion of the PCTA, it was later learned that a missing easement in the [[Stevens Pass]] (Washington) area threatened the continuity of the trail. A private landowner had been considering fencing off a segment of trail and cutting off public access. In 2017 the Pacific Crest Trail Association bought more than 400 acres for $1.6 million to keep the trail open to the public.{{Cite web|date=Nov 18, 2017|title=Group Buys Land to Prevent Break in Pacific Crest Trail|url=https://www.kgw.com/article/news/local/group-buys-land-to-prevent-break-in-pacific-crest-trail/492939354|website=Associated Press (KGW)|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/https://www.kgw.com/article/news/local/group-buys-land-to-prevent-break-in-pacific-crest-trail/492939354|url-status=live}} == The ''Wild'' phenomenon == [[Cheryl Strayed]]’s book, ''Wild,'' was published in 2012 and became a best-seller; the effect on the trail was initially modest with a small increase in inquiries to the PCTA. But in 2014, a movie based on the book came out, and had a much larger effect. According to a 2015 [[Associated Press]] article (which was published in newspapers throughout the United States, e.g.: the ''[[New York Daily News]]'',{{Cite news|last=Associated Press|date=Jan 20, 2015|title=The 'Wild' effect: Pacific Crest Trail expects more hikers thanks to movie|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/life-style/wild-effect-pacific-crest-trail-expects-hikers-article-1.2085376|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129044619/https://www.nydailynews.com/life-style/wild-effect-pacific-crest-trail-expects-hikers-article-1.2085376|url-status=live}} the [[The Santa Fe New Mexican|''Santa Fe New Mexican'']],{{Cite news|last=Harpaz|first=Beth J.|date=Jan 20, 2015|title=Pacific Crest Trail expects more hikers thanks to 'Wild'|work=The Santa Fe New Mexican|url=https://www.santafenewmexican.com/life/travel/pacific-crest-trail-expects-more-hikers-thanks-to-wild/article_1ca7c354-2c66-52e4-a38c-f2042e4c40a9.html|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/https://www.santafenewmexican.com/life/travel/pacific-crest-trail-expects-more-hikers-thanks-to-wild/article_1ca7c354-2c66-52e4-a38c-f2042e4c40a9.html|url-status=live}} and ''[[The Florida Times-Union]]''),{{Cite news|last=Harpaz|first=Beth J.|date=January 20, 2015|title=Thanks to 'Wild,' more hikers expected on Pacific Crest Trail|work=The Florida Times Union via Associated Press|url=https://www.jacksonville.com/story/entertainment/local/2015/01/20/thanks-wild-more-hikers-expected-pacific-crest-trail/15647735007/|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/https://www.jacksonville.com/story/entertainment/local/2015/01/20/thanks-wild-more-hikers-expected-pacific-crest-trail/15647735007/|url-status=live}} the PCTA saw a dramatic increase in the number of hikers attempting to hike the entire trail. Liz Bergeron, executive director of the Pacific Crest Trail Association, told [[Condé Nast Traveler|Conde Nast Traveler]] that the PCTA saw increased numbers everywhere within a year of the movie's release—more day hikers, doubled website traffic, and more permit requests for thru-hiking; she said that nearly 2,000 people attempted a thru-hike in 2014, double the previous year.{{Cite news|last=Williams|first=Allison|date=February 4, 2015|title=The 'Wild' Effect: How Cheryl Strayed's Memoir Inspires Hikers|work=Conde Nast Traveler|url=https://www.cntraveler.com/stories/2015-02-04/the-wild-effect-how-cheryl-strayeds-memoir-inspires-hikers|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2022-01-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220103225610/https://www.cntraveler.com/stories/2015-02-04/the-wild-effect-how-cheryl-strayeds-memoir-inspires-hikers|url-status=live}} In response, the PCTA launched a campaign, with Strayed's support, using the hashtag #responsiblywild to promote safety and Leave No Trace practices.{{Cite web|date=January 20, 2015|title=Wild Movie Boosts Number of PCT Hikers|url=https://www.outsideonline.com/outdoor-adventure/wild-movie-boosts-number-pct-hikers/|website=Outside Online|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/https://www.outsideonline.com/outdoor-adventure/wild-movie-boosts-number-pct-hikers/|url-status=live}} They also implemented a new permit system to limit the number of long-distance backpackers in order to spread out the usage.{{Cite web|last=Floro|first=Kelly|date=October 7, 2021|title=PACIFIC CREST TRAIL: How To Score a PCT Long-distance Permit|url=https://thetrek.co/pacific-crest-trail/how-to-score-a-pct-long-distance-permit/|website=The Trek|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/https://thetrek.co/pacific-crest-trail/how-to-score-a-pct-long-distance-permit/|url-status=live}} Speaking to ''Seattle Backpackers Magazine'', Bob Woods, the [[North Cascades]] Regional Director for the Pacific Crest Trail Association, explained that the new permit regulations were necessary because it was anticipated that the increased awareness of the trail would result in record breaking use in the next few years.{{Cite web|last=Franz|first=Dutch|date=February 6, 2015|title=The Movie Wild Spurs New Permitting System on the Pacific Crest Trail|url=https://seattlebackpackersmagazine.com/movie-wild-spurs-new-permitting-system-pacific-crest-trail/|website=Seattle Backpackers Magazine|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/https://seattlebackpackersmagazine.com/movie-wild-spurs-new-permitting-system-pacific-crest-trail/|url-status=live}} The PCTA also published information about the benefits of southbound itineraries, which could help to lessen the impact by spreading out hikers.{{Cite web|title=Pacific Crest Trail Association Southbound Guide|url=https://backpackers.com/blog/pacific-crest-trail-association-southbound-guide/|website=Backpackers|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2022-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/https://backpackers.com/blog/pacific-crest-trail-association-southbound-guide/|url-status=live}} == COVID-19 and the PCT == Immediately subsequent to the increase of traffic on the trail after the ''Wild'' phenomenon, the PCTA took a leading role in determining how trail policies would respond to the COVID-19 pandemic. Outdoor spaces nationwide saw a large uptick of visitor use by people looking for safe spaces in which to recreate.{{Cite web|last=Garth|first=Gary|date=Sep 6, 2020|title='Busiest camping season': Travelers choose outdoor recreation close to home amid COVID-19 pandemic|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/travel/destinations/2020/09/06/camping-rises-popularity-amid-covid-19-travel-concerns-south-dakota/5702412002/|website=USA Today|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043116/https://www.usatoday.com/story/travel/destinations/2020/09/06/camping-rises-popularity-amid-covid-19-travel-concerns-south-dakota/5702412002/|url-status=live}} But in April 2020, the PCTA asked long-distance hikers to postpone their 2020 thru-hikers, or, if they had already started, to leave the trail.{{Cite news|last=Burbank|first=Megan|date=Mar 20, 2020|title=Citing potential spread of coronavirus on Pacific Crest Trail and elsewhere, outdoor advocates urge thru-hikers to cancel plans|work=The Seattle Times|url=https://www.seattletimes.com/life/outdoors/citing-potential-spread-of-coronavirus-on-pacific-crest-trail-and-elsewhere-outdoor-advocates-urge-thru-hikers-to-cancel-plans/|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043117/https://www.seattletimes.com/life/outdoors/citing-potential-spread-of-coronavirus-on-pacific-crest-trail-and-elsewhere-outdoor-advocates-urge-thru-hikers-to-cancel-plans/|url-status=live}}{{Cite news|last=Hale|first=Jamie|date=Mar 20, 2020|title=Pacific Crest Trail hikers told to stay home during coronavirus outbreak|work=The Oregonian|url=https://www.oregonlive.com/coronavirus/2020/03/pacific-crest-trail-hikers-told-to-stay-home-during-coronavirus-outbreak.html|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/https://www.oregonlive.com/coronavirus/2020/03/pacific-crest-trail-hikers-told-to-stay-home-during-coronavirus-outbreak.html|url-status=live}} The PCTA was concerned about the potential for the virus to spread among hikers, because the trail is, in part, a social experience, and hikers often congregate close together.{{Cite news|last=Neumann|first=Erik|date=Apr 10, 2020|title='Heartbreaking' Guidance Calls For Hikers To Quit Pacific Crest Trail Trips Because Of Coronavirus|work=Jefferson Public Radio|url=https://www.ijpr.org/environment/2020-04-10/heartbreaking-guidance-calls-for-hikers-to-quit-pacific-crest-trail-trips-because-of-coronavirus|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2022-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043128/https://www.ijpr.org/environment/2020-04-10/heartbreaking-guidance-calls-for-hikers-to-quit-pacific-crest-trail-trips-because-of-coronavirus|url-status=usurped}} Long-distance hikers were also viewed as potential disease vectors who could spread the virus to rural communities with limited medical facilities that were already strained.{{Cite web|last=Roy|first=Adam|date=Mar 20, 2020|title=Pacific Crest Trail Association Asks Thru-Hikers to Cancel Their Trips Due to COVID-19|url=https://www.backpacker.com/news-and-events/pacific-crest-trail-association-asks-thru-hikers-to-cancel-their-trips-due-to-covid-19/|website=Backpacker|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043120/https://www.backpacker.com/news-and-events/pacific-crest-trail-association-asks-thru-hikers-to-cancel-their-trips-due-to-covid-19/|url-status=live}} Additionally, the PCTA was concerned about the inherent dangers of PCT hiking; the trail crosses high mountains and harsh environments, and at least 15 people have died on the trail, nine of them from either falls or heatstroke.{{Cite web|title=List of Deaths on the Pacific Crest Trail|url=https://www.halfwayanywhere.com/trails/pacific-crest-trail/list-of-deaths-on-the-pacific-crest-trail/|website=Halfway Anywhere|access-date=2022-01-29|archive-date=2022-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043118/https://www.halfwayanywhere.com/trails/pacific-crest-trail/list-of-deaths-on-the-pacific-crest-trail/|url-status=live}} The PCTA judged that it was more responsible to avoid the kinds of accidents that could require emergency services to operate in the wilderness environment, which could expose both victims and rescuers to the virus from necessary contact with each other, and which would take health workers away from much needed jobs on the front lines of the pandemic.{{Cite web|last=Fieldstadt|first=Elisha|date=Apr 1, 2020|title=One death, multiple rescues on Pacific Crest Trail heighten calls to stay away during pandemic|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/one-death-multiple-rescues-pacific-crest-trail-heighten-calls-stay-n1173856|website=NBC News|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129043116/https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/one-death-multiple-rescues-pacific-crest-trail-heighten-calls-stay-n1173856|url-status=live}} While the PCTA has no legal authority to close the trail, it does have the authority to grant permits for long-distance trips. In August 2020, the PCTA again delayed the opening of the permit cycle for 2021.{{Cite news|last=Neumann|first=Erik|date=Apr 26, 2020|title=Pacific Crest Trail Association Postpones 2021 Permits|work=Oregon Public Broadcasting|url=https://www.opb.org/article/2020/08/26/pacific-crest-trail-association-postpones-2021-permits|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220129082123/https://www.opb.org/article/2020/08/26/pacific-crest-trail-association-postpones-2021-permits/|url-status=live}} == References == {{reflist}} == External links == * [https://www.pcta.org/ Pacific Crest Trail Association] {{authority control}} [[Category:Hiking organizations in the United States]] [[Category:Environmental organizations based in the United States]]
extract: The Pacific Crest Trail Association (PCTA) is a nonprofit organization dedicated to the conservation and management of the Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail (usually abbreviated as the PCT), a 2,650-mile hiking and equestrian trail in the western United States that runs through California, Oregon, and Washington. The southern terminus is in Campo, California at the Mexican border approximately 50 miles east of San Diego. The northern terminus is at the US–Canadian border at E.C. Manning Provincial Park, which lies just north of the border between Washington and British Columbia.
